title: Operation Lukavac 93: The Battle for Igman and the First NATO Ultimatum
content:
In late July 1993, the VRS launched Operation Lukavac 93, a major offensive targeting Mount Igman and the Bjelasnica plateau southwest of Sarajevo. The operation's objective was to sever the last overland route connecting the besieged capital to government-held territory in central Bosnia -- the same route that the recently completed tunnel beneath the airport had been built to supplement. If the VRS could seize the Igman road, Sarajevo's isolation would be total, and the tunnel's value would be negated by the loss of the free territory it connected to.

The offensive committed substantial VRS forces, comprising thousands of troops, drawn primarily from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and reinforced with elements from other formations. The ARBiH defenders on Igman and Bjelasnica were significantly outnumbered. By early August, VRS units had captured key positions on Bjelasnica and cut the Igman road, bringing Sarajevo to the brink of complete encirclement. For several days, the city's last supply corridor was effectively closed.

The ICTY Mladic Trial Judgment (IT-09-92-T) addressed the Igman offensive within its broader examination of the siege of Sarajevo and the VRS command structure. The judgment documented the operation as part of the sustained campaign to maintain military pressure on the Bosnian capital, a campaign the tribunal found was directed at the highest levels of the Bosnian Serb military leadership.

What distinguished Operation Lukavac 93 from the many other VRS operations around Sarajevo was the international response it provoked. The offensive coincided with a period of growing frustration among Western governments over the impotence of the UN presence in Bosnia and the continued suffering of Sarajevo's civilian population. The seizure of Igman -- an action that threatened to produce a humanitarian catastrophe in a city already enduring extreme deprivation -- triggered the most forceful diplomatic intervention of the war to that date. NATO governments, led by the United States, issued explicit threats of air strikes against VRS positions if the offensive was not reversed.

This was not the first time air strikes had been discussed, but it was the first occasion on which the threat carried genuine credibility. The political dynamics had shifted sufficiently that the Bosnian Serb leadership could no longer assume that NATO would confine itself to rhetoric. Under pressure from both the international community and from Belgrade -- where Slobodan Milosevic was increasingly concerned about the costs of supporting Bosnian Serb intransigence -- the VRS command agreed to withdraw from Igman and Bjelasnica under a UN-brokered agreement concluded on 14 August 1993. UN forces were deployed to the vacated positions to monitor compliance.

The withdrawal was a significant moment in the war's trajectory. For the VRS, it represented the first instance in which a successful military operation was reversed not by opposing force on the ground but by the threat of external intervention. The lesson was ambiguous: it demonstrated that international pressure could compel a retreat, but it also revealed how high a threshold had to be crossed before that pressure materialized. The VRS had operated with near-impunity for over a year before encountering a credible ultimatum.

For the ARBiH and Sarajevo's population, the crisis and its resolution offered both relief and frustration. The immediate threat of total isolation was averted, and the Igman road -- though remaining under periodic fire -- was reopened. Yet the episode underscored how dependent Sarajevo's survival was on factors entirely outside its own control. The city had been saved not by its own military capacity but by a shift in the political calculus of distant capitals.

The Igman crisis also established a pattern that would recur throughout the remainder of the war: VRS overreach provoking international threats, followed by tactical withdrawal, followed by a return to the baseline of siege and attrition. The fundamental dynamics of the conflict remained unchanged, but the precedent of a credible NATO ultimatum had been set.
